title: How Knights Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how knights worked in medieval Europe, starting with the post-Roman chaos and the feudal system under Charlemagne, then covering the path from page (age seven) to squire (around fourteen) to knight (around twenty-one), the squire roles, the knightly oath and code of chivalry, weapons and armor (leather, chainmail, plate), tournaments and jousting, the Crusades' influence, orders such as the Knights Templar, Knights Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights and Order of the Garter, female knights, honorary knighthoods, and how gunpowder ended knighthood. The episode closes with trivia event announcements and listener Facebook questions.
topics: gunpowder and the end of knights

segments.title: Opening banter and setup
segments.summary: Hosts banter about a lack of current knight news, then decide to cover the history of knights starting after the fall of the Roman Empire.

segments.title: Post-Roman chaos and feudalism
segments.summary: After the Roman Empire fell, Western Europe was lawless. Charlemagne granted land to allies in exchange for military service, creating feudalism, with nobles, vassals, and serfs. Knighthood arose from this system.

segments.title: Becoming a knight: page and squire
segments.summary: Knighthood was earned, not inherited. Boys became pages around age seven, serving a lord's household and training, then squires around age fourteen. The word knight traces to an Old English word for boy.

segments.title: Squire roles and knightly training
segments.summary: The hosts describe the different squire jobs, such as carving, wine, pantry, arms, and honor squires. Squires were also trained in martial skills and wearing chainmail.

segments.title: Dubbing, the knightly oath, and code of chivalry
segments.summary: Squires became knights around age twenty-one, usually at a feast or festival, by being touched with a sword. Knights swore oaths including defending ladies, speaking truth, loyalty, devotion to the church, and defending the helpless. The code of chivalry came from the French word chevalerie and was meant to restrain powerful knights.

segments.title: Weapons and privileges of knights
segments.summary: Knights used lances and swords, with weapons like the warhammer and mace discussed. Archers were seen as cowardly by many knights. Knights gained privileges such as owning land, dispensing local justice, carrying swords into church, and sitting at high tables.

segments.title: Crusades and the romanticization of knights
segments.summary: The first Crusade in 1096 shaped knighthood, tying it to Christianity and popular romance. Orders of knights developed from the Crusades. The hosts say a full episode on the Crusades is needed.

segments.title: Peacetime tournaments, melee, and jousting
segments.summary: During peacetime knights held tournaments. The melee was a mock battle, and jousting scoring and ransom of armor and horses were discussed. King Henry the Second of France died from a joust injury. Ulrich von Liechtenstein is mentioned as a famous jousting knight who wrote an autobiography.

segments.title: Armor and gunpowder's end of knighthood
segments.summary: Leather, chainmail, and plate armor are compared; the hosts say chainmail was developed by Celts, not Romans. Gunpowder made armored mounted knights obsolete, paralleling the end of the samurai.

segments.title: Orders of knights and honorary knighthoods
segments.summary: Orders discussed include the Knights Templar, Knights Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights, and the Order of the Garter, which had women in it at one time. Women such as Order of the Hatchet members and Warrior Nuns are mentioned. Modern honorary knights include Elton John and others.

segments.title: Trivia event announcement and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts announce an October 2010 trivia event in Atlanta with John Hodgeman, Joe Randazzo, and Paul Tompkins-free lineup, then answer Facebook questions about the show and concerts and Halloween costumes.
